newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong protest leader had not planned to die.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong protest leader had not planned to die.

text.p: David Chan held aloft China's red national flag, the one he intended to plant on a disputed East China Sea islet, and led his band of supporters in a rendition of the Chinese national anthem.

Minutes later he stepped aboard a rusty tanker and set sail for the islands over which he was determined to assert China's sovereignty. "We will not retreat," Chan told Reuters, just before he began his voyage to the islands last Sunday.
That act of defiance led to Chan's death on Thursday and made him the first casualty in a growing chorus of protests by Chinese communities in Hong Kong, Taiwan, China and Macau.
Chan laid careful plans for the voyage in the Kien Hwa 2 to the cluster of tiny islands which Japan calls the Senkaku group and which China claims as the Diaoyu isles.

The leader of the somewhat motley array of 18 activists planned to play a game of maritime cat-and-mouse with a fleet of Japanese coastguard vessels and to storm the islands and tear down a makeshift lighthouse built by Japanese rightwingers.
"We will use every tactic and every strategy...to dodge the Japanese patrol boats and get on to those islands to raise the Chinese flag and restore our sovereignty," he said.

The 45-year-old media consultant and father of two was a seasoned street activist, donning a colourful headband and brandishing placards during recent demonstrations accusing the Japanese of invading the islands.
But even Chan knew that trying to out-manoeuvre the Japanese coastguard on two Zodiac inflatable dinghies badly in need of repair was a dangerous, even reckless mission.

If Chan was prepared to be a martyr, he gave no indication. "We know this could be dangerous, but this is Chinese territory, and we have every right to land there," he said confidently at the start of the voyage.
"We are civilians, we have no weapons, no explosives, and our ship is only a cargo ship, it's not armed. We will not retreat," Chan said.
Within 24 hours of reaching the waters around the disputed islands northeast of Taiwan, the Kien Hwa 2 was hemmed in by up to 20 Japanese coast guard vessels.
Earlier in the day, stormy seas had forced the protest ship to abandon efforts to land.
Chan made a last gesture of defiance.
Shackled to his ship by a length of rope that the men had evidently thought would keep them safe in rough seas, Chan and four other activists leapt into the sea.
Efforts to rescue Chan were hampered when he lost consciousness as he was dragged in the wake of the vessel.
In a supreme irony, a Japanese medical team boarded the Kien Hwa 2 to try to revive Chan, whose body had been hauled on deck nearly an hour after he jumped overboard.
"A doctor from Japan who boarded the Hong Kong ship confirmed that Chan Yuk Cheung David was dead," a spokesman for Japan's Maritime Safety Agency said.
